examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. The problem of avoiding duplicate names—such as for Internet domain names or for e-mail accounts—is particularly ______ when the name has to fit into a format that allows only a finite number of possibilities. Choices: A meager, B acute, C agreeable, D severe, E beneficial, F productive.

solution.operation: Read what the sentence says the blank must describe: the challenge of ensuring unique names under stated limitations
solution.result: The blank characterizes a problem, not a benefit
solution.description: Locate the noun the blank modifies — the problem of avoiding duplicate names — so you know the blank has to say something about a difficulty.

solution.operation: Use the 'when the name has to fit into a format that allows only a finite number of possibilities' clause as the directional clue
solution.result: The limitation adds to the difficulty, so the blank must reflect the arduousness of the task
solution.description: Read the closing clause: it names a restriction that makes duplicate-avoidance harder, which fixes the required meaning of the blank as 'intensely difficult'.

solution.operation: Test each choice against the required meaning 'arduous / intensified difficulty'
solution.result: acute and severe both indicate the added difficulty of the problem; meager, agreeable, beneficial and productive do not describe that difficulty
solution.description: Screen the six options one by one, keeping only those that characterize the problem as harder under the described circumstances and discarding the four that do not describe difficulty at all.

solution.operation: Check that the two surviving words produce completed sentences alike in meaning
solution.result: acute and severe form a matched pair yielding sentences with similar meanings
solution.description: Apply the Sentence Equivalence requirement to the survivors: substitute each into the sentence and confirm the two completed sentences say the same thing, which they do.

examples.answer: Choice B: acute; AND Choice D: severe

key_reminders: Sentence Equivalence needs two choices that both fit AND yield sentences alike in meaning.
The blank's direction is set by the clue clause — here, a limitation that increases difficulty.
A word that fits grammatically but has no synonym among the options cannot be part of the answer.
common_mistakes: Choosing a positively-valenced option such as agreeable, beneficial or productive when the clue clause describes an aggravating restriction.
Picking meager on the idea that a 'finite number of possibilities' is small, when the blank modifies the problem rather than the supply of names.

concept.technique_name: boldface role analysis (4-step Critical Reasoning process)

examples.problem_statement: Answer using the 4-step Critical Reasoning process. Innovative Design: Products with innovative and appealing designs relative to competing products can often command substantially higher prices in the marketplace. Because design innovations are quickly copied by other manufacturers, many consumer technology companies charge as much as possible for their new designs to extract as much value as possible from them. But large profits generated by the innovative designs give competitors stronger incentives to copy the designs. Therefore, the best strategy to maximize overall profit from an innovative new design is to charge less than the greatest possible price. In the argument above, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles? (A) The first is an assumption that supports a described course of action; the second provides a consideration to support a preferred course of action. (B) The first is a consideration that helps explain the appeal of a certain strategy; the second presents an alternative strategy endorsed by the argument. (C) The first is a phenomenon that makes a specific strategy unlikely to be successful; the second is that strategy. (D) The first is a consideration that demonstrates why a particular approach is flawed; the second describes a way to amend that approach. (E) The first is a factor used to rationalize a particular strategy; the second is a factor against that strategy.

solution.operation: Identify the question type from the wording 'the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles'
solution.result: This is a Role question — find the function of each bold statement
solution.description: Step 1 of the process: read the question stem first and classify it; the word boldface plus 'roles' marks it as a Describe the Role question.

solution.operation: Map sentence 1: innovative designs command substantially higher prices
solution.result: Between a fact and a claim — probably a premise; noted as 'Innov designs → higher price'
solution.description: Begin Step 2, deconstructing the argument: label the opening statement, which reads as background support rather than as anything the author is arguing for.

solution.operation: Map sentence 2: because innovations are quickly copied, many companies charge as much as possible
solution.result: Claim-based material whose first half supports its second half; not yet confirmed as the conclusion
solution.description: Label the second sentence, noticing the internal because-structure that makes the first half support the charge-maximum strategy stated in the second half.

solution.operation: Map sentence 3, opening with 'But': large profits give competitors stronger incentives to copy
solution.result: Contrast — a drawback of making very large profits
solution.description: Register the BUT as a pivot: the author is introducing a downside to the charge-the-maximum approach just described.

solution.operation: Map sentence 4, opening with 'Therefore': the best strategy is to charge less than the greatest possible price
solution.result: This is the conclusion; the second boldface = C (conclusion)
solution.description: Identify the conclusion from the Therefore signal and assign the second boldface its role — it is the strategy the argument itself endorses.

solution.operation: Assign the first boldface its role given that conclusion
solution.result: A premise supporting the rival strategy (charge the greatest possible price) that the argument disagrees with; labelled X
solution.description: Back-fill the first boldface's role: since the author argues against charging the maximum, the opening statement functions as support for the strategy the author opposes.

solution.operation: State the goal: find an answer giving X then C, in that order
solution.result: Want: premise supporting the alternate strategy, then the argument's own conclusion
solution.description: Step 3 of the process: fix the target before reading the choices, so each option is judged against a pre-set standard rather than reconsidered from scratch.

solution.operation: Test (A): first as an assumption supporting a described course of action; second as a consideration supporting a preferred course of action
solution.result: Eliminate — 'assumption' is tolerable, but the second is the actual conclusion, not another supporting consideration
solution.description: Step 4 begins, working from wrong to right: reject (A) because it demotes the conclusion to the status of a premise.

solution.operation: Test (B): first as a consideration explaining the appeal of a certain strategy; second as an alternative strategy endorsed by the argument
solution.result: Keep — the first does support the greatest-possible-price strategy, and the second is the strategy the argument supports
solution.description: Check (B) against the X-then-C target: the awkwardly worded first half still describes a premise backing the rival strategy, and the second half names the author's endorsed strategy.

solution.operation: Test (C): first as a phenomenon making a specific strategy unlikely to succeed
solution.result: Eliminate — the first boldface supports the first strategy rather than weakening any strategy
solution.description: Reject (C) because it casts the first boldface as an objection, whereas it actually provides support.

solution.operation: Test (D) and (E): (D) first demonstrates why an approach is flawed; (E) second is a factor against that strategy
solution.result: Eliminate both — (D) misreads the first boldface as illustrating a flaw; (E) misreads the second boldface as opposing the strategy when it is the author's own strategy
solution.description: Clear the last two choices on their decisive halves: (D) fails on its first half, so the second half need not be read, and (E) fails because the second boldface is the endorsed strategy, not an argument against one.

key_reminders: Find the conclusion first — Therefore marks it — then define each boldface relative to it.
A boldface that supports a strategy the author rejects is still a premise, just a premise for the opposing side.
Eliminate a choice as soon as one half misdescribes its boldface; the other half need not be read.
common_mistakes: Treating the second boldface (the Therefore sentence) as supporting evidence rather than as the argument's conclusion, which is what makes (A) tempting.
Assuming the first boldface opposes the author's strategy because the author ultimately disagrees with charging the maximum — the trap in (C) and (D).

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion via clue words

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. The lizards snapped up insects that are so (i) ______ that other potential predators avoid them. Among the lizards’ prey were some beetles that they initially (ii) ______ because the insects were spraying their hot, irritant defense chemical at the time. Yet even these produced no apparent ill effects, since the lizards, having eaten, proceeded on their way (iii) ______ enough. Blank (i): A rare, B nutritious, C noxious. Blank (ii): D sought, E rejected, F resembled. Blank (iii): G erratically, H laboriously, I nonchalantly.

solution.operation: Read what Blank (i) must describe: insects that other potential predators avoid
solution.result: The blank needs a word meaning harmful — 'noxious'
solution.description: Set the requirement for the first blank from the clause that follows it: predators avoid these insects, so the adjective must give a reason for avoidance.

solution.operation: Test the other Blank (i) options, rare and nutritious, against that requirement
solution.result: Eliminated — there is no reason to suspect predators would avoid rare or nutritious prey
solution.description: Reject the two rivals in column (i) because neither property would cause a predator to stay away.

solution.operation: Read Blank (ii) as the lizards' initial response to beetles they eventually ate, explained by the following 'because' clause about irritant spraying
solution.result: The response must be caused by the spraying — 'rejected' fits, since animals routinely avoid unpleasant stimuli
solution.description: Use the because-clause as the causal clue for the second blank: whatever the lizards did at first has to be a reaction to being sprayed with an irritant.

solution.operation: Test the other Blank (ii) options, sought and resembled
solution.result: Eliminated — lizards are unlikely to seek out prey with such defensive behavior, and nothing in the passage suggests the lizards share that behavior
solution.description: Discard the two rivals in column (ii): one contradicts the causal clue, the other imports a similarity the passage never mentions.

solution.operation: Read Blank (iii) through the 'since' clause, which supplies the evidence that eating the beetles did not harm the lizards
solution.result: The blank must describe post-meal movement suggesting the lizards were unharmed
solution.description: Identify what the third blank has to prove: since introduces the evidence for the claim of no ill effects, so the manner word must signal that the lizards were fine.

solution.operation: Test the Blank (iii) options against 'unharmed'
solution.result: Erratic or laborious locomotion would indicate the opposite, so 'nonchalantly' is correct
solution.description: Compare the three manner adverbs: two would be signs of distress and therefore contradict the sentence's claim, leaving the one that conveys unconcerned normality.

examples.answer: Choice C: noxious; Choice E: rejected; Choice I: nonchalantly

key_reminders: Each blank is fixed by an explicit connector: 'so...that' for (i), 'because' for (ii), 'since' for (iii).
The 'since' clause supplies evidence for the preceding claim, so blank (iii) must be consistent with no ill effects.
Fill the blank with the strongest clue first; the columns are independent, so a wrong choice in one does not force another.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'sought' for blank (ii) by reading 'snapped up' as eagerness, ignoring that the because-clause explains a deterrent.
Choosing 'erratically' or 'laboriously' for blank (iii) because the beetles sprayed an irritant, which reverses the sentence's stated finding of no ill effects.

concept.technique_name: fourth power by tabular column method with multipliers 3, 5, 3

examples.problem_statement: Using the Fourth Power Computation technique of Vedic Mathematics (tabular approach with specific coefficients): base number = 11, a = 1, b = 1, ratio b/a = 1, multipliers = 3, 5, 3. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: Identify the number to be raised to the fourth power: (11)^4
solution.result: Target is 11^4
solution.description: Write down what is being computed so the tabular layout is set up for a fourth power rather than a square or cube.

solution.operation: Set a = 1 and b = 1, the digits of 11
solution.description: Split the base number into its two parts a and b, which are the values the whole table will be built from.

solution.operation: Calculate the ratio b/a = 1/1
solution.result: ratio = 1
solution.description: Form the ratio of the second part to the first; it is the factor used to step from one column to the next.

solution.operation: Write the fourth power of a in the first column: 1^4
solution.result: First column = 1
solution.description: Seed the table with a^4 in the leftmost column, which anchors the row of five entries.

solution.operation: Fill the remaining four columns by repeatedly multiplying by the ratio: 1 \times 1 in each column
solution.result: Row reads 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
solution.description: Propagate across the table by multiplying each entry by the ratio 1, giving the base row before the coefficients are applied.

solution.operation: Multiply the second column digit by 3: 1 \times 3
solution.description: Apply the first of the fixed multipliers 3, 5, 3 to the second column, producing the extra amount to be added there.

solution.operation: Multiply the third column digit by 5: 1 \times 5
solution.description: Apply the middle multiplier 5 to the third column, the largest coefficient in the pattern.

solution.operation: Multiply the fourth column digit by 3: 1 \times 3
solution.description: Apply the last multiplier 3 to the fourth column, mirroring what was done to the second column.

solution.operation: Add each column separately: [1], [1+3], [1+5], [1+3], [1]
solution.description: Sum the base row entry and the multiplier-derived entry within each column independently, keeping the five columns separate.

solution.operation: Read the result off the columns: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1
solution.description: Concatenate the column totals in order to read the final answer, since no column total exceeds 9 and therefore no carrying is required.

examples.answer: The fourth power of 11 is 14641, calculated using Vedic Mathematics tabular method with multipliers 3, 5, and 3 applied to columns.

key_reminders: The fourth-power table has five columns, seeded with a^4 and extended by the ratio b/a.
The fixed multipliers for the inner columns are 3, 5, 3 in that order.
Column totals are read off left to right as digits.
common_mistakes: Applying a multiplier to the first or fifth column; only the three inner columns take the 3, 5, 3 coefficients.
Ordering the multipliers as 3, 3, 5 rather than the symmetric 3, 5, 3, which would give 1, 4, 4, 6, 1 instead of 14641.

concept.technique_name: two-blank text completion via contrast clues

examples.problem_statement: Indicate the best answer for each blank. There is nothing quite like this movie, and indeed I am not altogether sure there is much more to it than its lovely (i) ______ . At a moment when so many films strive to be as (ii) ______ as possible, it is gratifying to find one that is so subtle and puzzling. Blank (i): A peculiarity, B pellucidity, C conventionality. Blank (ii): D indirect, E assertive, F enigmatic.

solution.operation: Collect the two descriptions the sentences give of the movie: 'nothing quite like it' and 'subtle and puzzling'
solution.result: Two clues that any choice must satisfy simultaneously
solution.description: Gather the explicit characterizations of the film before touching the columns, since both blanks are judged against these same clues.

solution.operation: Test Blank (i) options against 'nothing quite like it'
solution.result: 'Peculiarity' is a solid fit; 'conventionality' clearly does not work
solution.description: Match the first column to the uniqueness clue: a word meaning oddness fits, while a word meaning ordinariness directly contradicts it.

solution.operation: Test the remaining Blank (i) option, pellucidity, against 'subtle and puzzling'
solution.result: Eliminated — it could fit the first sentence in isolation but not the later claim that the movie is subtle and puzzling
solution.description: Check the surviving rival against the second clue rather than the first alone: clarity cannot describe a film the writer calls puzzling.

solution.operation: Read Blank (ii) as needing a contrast with 'subtle and puzzling'
solution.result: Only 'assertive' clearly provides that contrast, so it fills blank (ii)
solution.description: Use the contrast set up by 'it is gratifying to find one that is so subtle and puzzling' to require an opposite quality in the second blank, and pick the only option that supplies it.

examples.answer: Choice A: peculiarity; Choice E: assertive

key_reminders: A choice must fit every clue in the passage, not just the clause nearest the blank.
'At a moment when so many films strive to be...' sets up a contrast with the film being praised, so blank (ii) is the opposite of subtle and puzzling.
common_mistakes: Selecting 'pellucidity' for blank (i) because it reads as praise ('lovely'), overlooking that the movie is described as puzzling.
Selecting 'indirect' or 'enigmatic' for blank (ii), which restate 'subtle and puzzling' instead of contrasting with it.
